body.en: A series \(\sum a_n\) converges when its partial sums \(S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n\) approach a finite limit. Because closed-form summation formulas rarely exist for arbitrary series, mathematical analysis provides a hierarchy of rigorous convergence tests based on term asymptotics, comparative decay rates, and functional analogs. Furthermore, power series extend polynomials into infinite functional representations whose domains are governed by a characteristic radius of convergence.

label.en: ● Definition 11.0 — Precise (ε, N) Limit of a Sequence

body.en:
A sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges to a real limit \(L\), written \(\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L\), if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that:

\[ n > N \implies |a_n - L| < \varepsilon. \]

Geometric Meaning: No matter how narrow an error corridor \((L - \varepsilon, L + \varepsilon)\) is chosen around \(L\), there is a cutoff index \(N\) beyond which all subsequent terms \(a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \dots\) are trapped permanently inside the corridor.

body.en:
Example 1: Prove using the \(\varepsilon\text{--}N\) definition that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0\).

Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. By the Archimedean Property of the real numbers, choose an integer \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(N \ge \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil > 0\). For any integer \(n > N\): \[ \left|\frac{1}{n} - 0\right| = \frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{N} \le \varepsilon. \] Thus \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example 2: Prove that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} = \frac{3}{2}\).

1. Scratchwork: We examine the error: \[ \left|\frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} - \frac{3}{2}\right| = \left|\frac{2(3n - 1) - 3(2n + 5)}{2(2n + 5)}\right| = \left|\frac{6n - 2 - 6n - 15}{4n + 10}\right| = \frac{17}{4n + 10} < \frac{17}{4n}. \] We want \(\frac{17}{4n} < \varepsilon \iff 4n > \frac{17}{\varepsilon} \iff n > \frac{17}{4\varepsilon}\). Choose \(N = \lceil \frac{17}{4\varepsilon} \rceil\).

2. Formal Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. Select \(N = \max\left(1, \left\lceil \frac{17}{4\varepsilon} \right\rceil\right)\). For any \(n > N\): \[ \left|\frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} - \frac{3}{2}\right| = \frac{17}{4n + 10} < \frac{17}{4n} < \frac{17}{4N} \le \varepsilon. \] Hence \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} = \frac{3}{2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

body.en:
If the series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) converges, then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0\).

Equivalently (by contrapositive): If \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n \ne 0\) or fails to exist, then \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) diverges.

Critical Warning: The converse is FALSE! The condition \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0\) is necessary but NOT sufficient for convergence (e.g. the harmonic series \(\sum 1/n\) diverges even though \(1/n \to 0\)).

Analytical Proof

Let \(S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k\) denote the sequence of partial sums. If the series converges to a finite sum \(S\), then \(\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = S\) and \(\lim_{n \to \infty} S_{n-1} = S\).

For \(n \ge 2\), the \(n\)-th term is the difference of successive partial sums: \(a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}\).

Taking the limit of both sides as \(n \to \infty\):

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} (S_n - S_{n-1}) = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n - \lim_{n \to \infty} S_{n-1} = S - S = 0 \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: Worked Example 11.1 — Foundations: Divergence Test Application

body.en:
Determine whether the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3n^2 + 5}{7n^2 - 2n + 1}\) converges or diverges.

Step 1: Evaluate the limit of the nth term as \(n \to \infty\).

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3n^2 + 5}{7n^2 - 2n + 1} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3 + 5/n^2}{7 - 2/n + 1/n^2} = \frac{3 + 0}{7 - 0 + 0} = \frac{3}{7} \]

Step 2: Apply the Divergence Test.
Since \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \frac{3}{7} \ne 0\), by Theorem 11.1 the series diverges.

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations
Use the Divergence Test to determine whether \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\) converges or diverges.

solution.en:
Compute the limit of the general term as \(n \to \infty\):
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} \cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \cos\left( \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} \right) = \cos(0) = 1 \]
Because \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 1 \ne 0\), the series diverges by the Divergence Test.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 11.2 — The Integral Test and p-Series Convergence

body.en:
Let \(f(x)\) be continuous, positive, and decreasing on \([1, \infty)\), with \(a_n = f(n)\). Then:

\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \text{ converges} \iff \int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx \text{ converges} \]

The \(p\)-Series Theorem: The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}\) converges if and only if \(p > 1\). For \(p \le 1\), it diverges.

Analytical Proof via Riemann Partition Bounds

Because \(f(x)\) is decreasing on each interval \([i, i+1]\), the function satisfies \(f(i+1) \le f(x) \le f(i)\) for all \(x \in [i, i+1]\).

Integrating over \([i, i+1]\):

\[ a_{i+1} = f(i+1) \le \int_i^{i+1} f(x)\,dx \le f(i) = a_i \]

Summing from \(i = 1\) to \(N-1\):

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} a_{i+1} \le \int_1^N f(x)\,dx \le \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} a_i \implies S_N - a_1 \le \int_1^N f(x)\,dx \le S_{N-1} \]

This establishes two crucial bounds:

  • If \(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\) converges to \(I\), then \(S_N \le a_1 + I\). The sequence \(S_N\) is strictly increasing and bounded above, hence by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, \(\sum a_n\) converges.
  • If \(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\) diverges, then \(S_N \ge \int_1^N f(x)\,dx \to \infty\), so \(\sum a_n\) diverges \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: ▲ Theorem 11.3 — The Ratio and Alternating Series Tests

body.en:
The Ratio Test: Let \(\sum a_n\) be a series with nonzero terms, and let \(L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\):

  • If \(L < 1\), the series converges absolutely.
  • If \(L > 1\) (or \(L = \infty\)), the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\), the test is inconclusive (use comparison or integral tests).

The Alternating Series Test (Leibniz's Theorem): The alternating series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n-1} b_n\) (where \(b_n > 0\)) converges if:

  1. \(b_{n+1} \le b_n\) for all \(n\) (monotonic non-increasing), and
  2. \(\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n = 0\).

Moreover, the remainder error is bounded by the first omitted term: \(|S - S_N| \le b_{N+1}\).

label.en: Worked Example 11.2 — Medium: Ratio Test on Factorials and Exponentials

body.en:
Test \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n!}{4^n}\) for convergence.

Step 1: Compute ratio \(\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\).

\[ \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \frac{(n+1)!}{4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{4^n}{n!} = \frac{(n+1)n!}{4 \cdot 4^n} \cdot \frac{4^n}{n!} = \frac{n+1}{4} \]

Step 2: Evaluate limit \(L\).

\[ L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n+1}{4} = \infty > 1 \]

Since \(L = \infty > 1\), the series diverges by the Ratio Test.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium
Determine whether the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}}\) converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges.

solution.en:
Step 1: Test for absolute convergence.
Consider \(\sum |a_n| = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{1/2}}\).
This is a \(p\)-series with \(p = 1/2 \le 1\), which diverges. Hence the series does NOT converge absolutely.
Step 2: Apply Alternating Series Test.
Here \(b_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} > 0\).
1. Monotonicity: \(n+1 > n \implies \sqrt{n+1} > \sqrt{n} \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}} < \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\), so \(b_{n+1} \le b_n\).
2. Limit: \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} = 0\).
Both conditions hold, so \(\sum a_n\) converges.
Conclusion: The series is conditionally convergent.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 11.4 — Power Series Convergence & Interval of Convergence

body.en:
For any power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n(x - a)^n\) centered at \(a\), exactly one of the following holds:

  1. The series converges only at \(x = a\) (radius \(R = 0\)).
  2. The series converges absolutely for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) (radius \(R = \infty\)).
  3. There exists a finite real number \(R > 0\) such that the series converges absolutely for \(|x - a| < R\) and diverges for \(|x - a| > R\).

Endpoint Testing: At the boundary endpoints \(x = a - R\) and \(x = a + R\), convergence cannot be determined by the Ratio Test (which always yields \(L = 1\)) and must be evaluated individually using other convergence tests.

label.en: Worked Example 11.3 — Advanced: Finding Full Interval of Convergence with Endpoint Analysis

body.en:
Find the radius of convergence \(R\) and the full interval of convergence \(I\) for \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(x - 2)^n}{n \cdot 3^n}\).

Step 1: Apply Ratio Test to determine radius \(R\).

\[ L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{(x - 2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)3^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n \cdot 3^n}{(x - 2)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{n+1} \cdot \frac{|x - 2|}{3} = 1 \cdot \frac{|x - 2|}{3} = \frac{|x - 2|}{3} \]

For absolute convergence, require \(L < 1\):

\[ \frac{|x - 2|}{3} < 1 \implies |x - 2| < 3 \implies -3 < x - 2 < 3 \implies -1 < x < 5 \]

Thus the radius of convergence is \(R = 3\).

Step 2: Test left endpoint \(x = -1\).
Substitute \(x = -1\):

\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1 - 2)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-3)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n 3^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n} \]

This is the alternating harmonic series, which converges by the Alternating Series Test.

Step 3: Test right endpoint \(x = 5\).
Substitute \(x = 5\):

\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(5 - 2)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n} \]

This is the divergent harmonic \(p\)-series (\(p = 1\)).

Conclusion: Radius \(R = 3\), Interval of Convergence \(I = [-1, 5)\).

Ratio Test Inconclusiveness (L = 1): If \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = 1\), the Ratio Test gives NO conclusion whatsoever. In particular, the Ratio Test ALWAYS gives \(L = 1\) for any p-series or rational fraction in \(n\); use the Comparison Test or Integral Test instead!

Testing Endpoints for Interval of Convergence: Finding the radius of convergence \(R\) determines an open interval \((a - R, a + R)\). You MUST test each endpoint \(x = a - R\) and \(x = a + R\) separately, as convergence at boundaries varies (e.g. one end might be conditionally convergent via Alternating Series while the other diverges).

Absolute vs Conditional Convergence: A series \(\sum a_n\) is conditionally convergent if \(\sum a_n\) converges, but \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges (classic example: \(\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\)).

Geometric Series Initial Index: Verify whether a geometric series begins at \(n = 0\) or \(n = 1\). The sum formula is always \(S = \frac{\text{First Term}}{1 - r}\); blindly writing \(\frac{a}{1 - r}\) when \(n\) starts at \(1\) or \(2\) results in an incorrect numerator.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced
Find the full interval of convergence (including endpoint behavior) for the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(2x - 1)^n}{n^2 \cdot 4^n}\).

solution.en:
Apply the Ratio Test:
\[ L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{(2x - 1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2 4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^2 4^n}{(2x - 1)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} = \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} \]
Require \(L < 1\):
\[ \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} < 1 \implies |2x - 1| < 4 \implies -4 < 2x - 1 < 4 \implies -3 < 2x < 5 \implies -\frac{3}{2} < x < \frac{5}{2} \]
The center is \(x = 1/2\) and radius is \(R = 2\).
Endpoint \(x = 5/2\): \(2x - 1 = 4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\), which converges by the \(p\)-series test (\(p = 2 > 1\)).
Endpoint \(x = -3/2\): \(2x - 1 = -4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-4)^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\), which converges absolutely (since \(\sum 1/n^2\) converges).
Therefore, the interval of convergence is \(\left[ -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right]\).

question.en: [Convergence Tests & Power Series · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
